lines.text: Don't help me up. I'm not up, I'm looking.
Forty-one years I've rung that bell at dusk. Forty-one. And tonight it won't sound — and it is not my hands, before you ask, because everyone has asked.
The clapper pin's sheared. The tongue's hanging in there like a dead thing. You could pull that rope till the small hours and get nothing but rope.

choices.text: Does it matter if it doesn't ring?

lines.text: To me? Not a scrap. I'd sleep.
To the ones still out past the ford it matters, because that bell is how they learn the light's going and they're further from a door than they thought.
It is not a magic bell. It is a loud one. That has always been enough.
You say it like it's a long time. It's a rope and a habit.
I've rung it through two floods, a fire, and the winter we don't talk about. I rang it the night my husband died, because it was dusk, and that is when you ring it.
So no. Tonight is not the night it stops.
Hobb can cut a new pin in an hour. He's done it before. That is rather the problem, but you'll get that out of him yourself or not at all.
What he hasn't got is iron worth trusting. Cart-band scrap will shear again by Tuesday and I will not be doing this twice.
There's good iron walking about out past the ford. It's on a bellow. It doesn't come off easy.
Because you're stood here with a sword on, and everyone else in this square is stood here with an opinion.
Good.
Take the boy off the step on your way. He's been leaving for three weeks and it's doing nobody any good, least of all him.
Is that it? Give it — no. You hold it. My hands, remember.
Up you go. The stair's sound, hold the inside, and when you reach the rope you will want to be clever about it.
Don't be. Put your weight on it and sit down. The bell knows its business.
And listen — count to three after. Everyone lets go on the one.
You'll hear why.
Light's going. I can see it going from here.
Don't. Whatever it is. I can see it on you from here.
You've got the walk. The one where somebody's handed you a job and you've decided it's yours now.

choices.text: The bell's broken. I need iron.
You've been on that step three weeks.

lines.text: Twenty-two days. But who's counting, besides me, constantly.
It's a good step. You can see everyone arrive and nobody sees you.
You'd be amazed what people do when they think the square's empty.
Bellow scale. Out past the ford.
You know what a bellow does when it's cornered? It doesn't run. That's the whole thing about them — they have never once in their lives considered it.
No. No, that is an unbelievably cheap trick and it has worked, so.
Right.
I've watched about four hundred people walk out that gate and I've got very good at guessing which ones come back.
I have never once had to guess about myself. I'd like to keep that record. Stay where I can see you.
Sit down. Watch a while. It's better than it looks.
I've heard that bell two thousand times.
First time I've heard it from under the rope.
Still here. Still regretting it at a steady rate.
Don't move — no, seriously, don't, you're standing on it.
There's a cut mark under your boot. Somebody dressed that stone. Somebody stood here with a chisel, made a decision about it, and then went home and had their dinner.
Sorry. Hello. What time is it?

choices.text: How long have you been out here?

lines.text: Since —
…since the light was on the other side of that wall, which is not the answer I wanted to arrive at.
Broken.
So nobody rang it, and nobody's going to, and I'd have sat out here until it was properly dark wondering why the evening felt wrong.
That's what it's for. I have never once thought about what it was for.
Absolutely not. You have just told me there's a reason to be somewhere.
Right. Bellow. Iron. Forge. Tower.
And then I am coming straight back out here, because that chisel mark has waited eight hundred years and it can wait one more night.
You know what I keep thinking? Somebody cast that bell. Somebody stood in a shed and decided how loud it needed to be.
They got it exactly right.
Still with you. Still not looking at that wall.
Let's see it.
…That'll do. That will more than do. Where'd you take it off, the shoulder?

choices.text: The Sexton said you'd done this before.

lines.text: She would.
Twenty-one years back. I cut that pin, I set it, and I stood in the square and listened to it ring and I thought: that's mine, that is. That's me, up there, going out over the whole valley.
A pin like that should do forty. It did twenty-one.
So you'll understand I have been sat here since noon not mending it. I'd rather you didn't repeat that.
Give me the fire and a quarter of an hour.
There. Don't look at it like that, it's a pin. A bit of iron with one job.
Get it up that tower before the light's gone and neither of us will have to think about it again.
It's in your hand. Tower's that way. Go on.
Don't lean on that. It's been hot since before you were up.
Bring me iron I can trust and we'll talk. Scrap shears. I have had enough of things shearing.
You're the one with the sword.
I'm Nell. I know four ways onto the roofs and one way under the square, and I'm not telling you the under one.

choices.text: Is everyone in for the night?

lines.text: I counted. Nobody asked me to. I just do it.
Everyone's in except the tall one who looks at walls. She went out at the second bell and she hasn't come back, and I told Tally, and Tally said she never does.
But she always comes back at the dusk bell. Always. And there isn't going to be one.
The gallery steps. Everyone finds those. Go up them and keep going up.
There's a lead that runs the whole east range. Somebody left something good at the far end and it's still there, so nobody has been all the way along.
I heard it. I was on the roof. I'm always on the roof.
She came back. I watched her come over the ford. I counted her in.
Mind the crates, mind the crates. You'd think a square this size would be room enough for four stalls and one cart, and you would be wrong.
Tally. I sell what the road brings in, which this month is apples and opinions.

choices.text: Those glowing things in the grass.

lines.text: Have a look. Mind the crates.
You noticed. Well, you would. You're new.
It's the bell. Nobody has said the word 'bell' to me all afternoon, and every one of them has come past and not said it, which takes effort.
You don't notice a sound until the evening it isn't there. Then you notice it in your chest.
Embercaps. They come up after rain along the walls and down the ravine, and they keep their light a good while after you knock them loose.
Children collect them. Grown adults with swords also collect them, and pretend it's for a reason.
There it is.
Forty-one years, and I have complained about that bell roughly every one of them. Loud thing. Rattles the jars.
Don't you dare tell anyone I cried at it.
Come in, come in — mind the step, everyone forgets the step.
Finn. If it isn't nailed down and isn't a sheep, I've probably had one through here.
Everything on the shelf and a few things under it. Take your time.
Nettles in the long grass, curlers by the water. Nothing you'd write home about.
There's a bellow up on the ridge, though, and it has got bolder this week. Comes down a little further every evening.
Take the tonics. Take two. I'd rather be wrong and out of pocket.
Back in. Mind the step.
Shut the gate behind you or I'll be up on the roofs after them all afternoon.
Mara. These four are the last of the town flock. The rest are out at the fold now the wall's mended.

choices.text: Do they come in on the bell?

lines.text: They do. Not because they're clever. Because it's loud, and they're startled, and the gate is open, and the gate is where startled goes.
Forty-one years of the same noise at the same hour. You can train anything on that. Sheep. People.
Drystone, four walls, gate downhill. Out past the ford, then west off the road where the rock spine runs.
Get up on the spine and look west and you'll see it below you, and the cairn on the rise above it. My grandfather stacked that cairn. Or said he did.
Gate. Thank you.
It's fine. It's fine. It only does that on the left.
Pip. Carter, when the cart agrees.
Out the gate, down through the fields, over the ford, and up. Keeps going up until it stops being worth it.
There's a cutting at the top with a beacon in it. I've had the cart that far exactly once and I'd not do it twice.
The gorge west of the road? Water cut it. You can get down into the bed if you pick your spot, and it's cool down there on a day like this.
Caps grow along the bottom. Mind the walk out — it's steeper than the walk in, which is always the way.
Still only on the left.
